title: A Simple, Effective Homework Plan For Teachers: Part 1 https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/07/31/effective-homework-plan-for-teachers-part-1/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In the first half of a two-part series, Linsin presents four strategies for eliminating the obstacles and excuses that undermine homework completion. He insists homework should only cover material students have already mastered during the school day, since assigning anything else unfairly shifts teaching duties onto parents at the dinner table. He advises deliberately excluding parents from the homework agreement, telling them at back-to-school night that any confusion is the teacher's responsibility to fix. Before dismissal, teachers should review the assignment and ask whether anyone anticipates being unable to turn it in the next day, closing off excuses in advance. Finally, incomplete homework should be confronted directly and calmly the next morning during a routine check, using personal leverage and peer awareness—not humiliation—to hold students accountable.
points: Only assign homework that covers material students have already fully mastered during the school day, since homework's purpose is practice, not new learning.
Keep parents out of the homework agreement so that the burden of clarity and follow-through rests entirely with the teacher and student.
Review homework before the end of the school day and ask if anyone anticipates being unable to turn it in the next morning, eliminating future excuses.
Check homework each morning without collecting it, using a routine that takes just seconds per student and flags widespread errors as a sign the lesson needs reteaching.
Confront incomplete homework on the spot the next morning calmly and without humiliation, relying on rapport and peer awareness as motivation.
quotes: Dealing with homework can be the source of great stress for teachers; it’s a rare week that I don’t receive at least one email asking for advice.

The skills needed to complete the evening’s homework must be thoroughly taught during the school day. If your students can’t prove to you that they’re able to do the work without assistance, then you shouldn’t assign it.
You should tell parents at back-to-school night, “I got it covered. If ever your child doesn’t understand the homework, it’s on me. Just send me a note and I’ll take care of it.
Is there anyone, for any reason, who will not be able to turn in their homework in the morning? I want to know now rather than find out about it in the morning.
If you see more than this, then you know your lesson was less than effective, and you’ll have to reteach.
The personal leverage you carry–that critical trusting rapport you have with your students–combined with the always lurking peer pressure is a powerful force.
